title: State, Events & Conditional Rendering
description: Make your components interactive. Learn useState for local state management, handle browser events the React way, conditionally render UI, and build dynamic lists — the essentials of every real React application.
learningObjectives: Add interactivity using the useState hook
Handle click, change, submit, and keyboard events
Conditionally render UI using &&, ternary, and early returns

sections.content: State is data that changes over time and causes the UI to update. Unlike props (set by parents), state is local to a component and managed by it. When state changes, React re-renders the component.  useState is the hook that adds state to function components.
⚠️ Never mutate state directly: count++ or state.items.push(). Always use the setter function. React compares references to detect changes — direct mutation bypasses this.

exercises.question: What happens when you call the state setter function (e.g., setCount)?
options: The variable updates immediately in the current render
React schedules a re-render with the new value
exercises.correctAnswer: React schedules a re-render with the new value
hints: State updates are asynchronous and batched
exercises.explanation: Calling a setter schedules a re-render. After the current event handler completes, React batches the updates and re-renders the component with the new state value. The current render's variables don't change.

sections.content: React wraps native DOM events in SyntheticEvents for cross-browser consistency. Event names use camelCase (onClick, onChange, onSubmit). You pass a function reference, not a string.

exercises.question: What's wrong with <button onClick={handleClick()}>Click</button>?
options: handleClick() with () calls it immediately on render, not on click
You can't use functions in JSX
The button needs a type attribute
exercises.correctAnswer: handleClick() with () calls it immediately on render, not on click
hints: What does () after a function name do?
exercises.explanation: onClick={handleClick()} immediately invokes handleClick during rendering and passes its return value (likely undefined) as the handler. You want onClick={handleClick} — passing the function reference.

sections.content: In a controlled component, React state is the single source of truth for input values. The input's value prop is tied to state; onChange updates state. This gives you full control to validate, transform, or react to input in real-time.

exercises.question: In a controlled input, what must always be provided alongside the value prop?
hints: If value is set but onChange is missing, React throws a warning
exercises.explanation: A controlled input with value but no onChange handler creates a read-only input that the user can't modify. onChange is required to update state and allow the user to type. React warns you if you forget it.

sections.content: ⚠️ Avoid: {count && <Component />} when count could be 0. '0 && anything' renders '0' in the DOM! Always use: {count > 0 && <Component />} or a ternary instead.

exercises.question: What does {items.length && <List />} render when items is an empty array?
hints: [].length is 0, and 0 is falsy but renderable
exercises.explanation: items.length returns 0 (a number). 0 && <List /> short-circuits to 0 — which React renders as the text '0' in the DOM! Use {items.length > 0 && <List />} or a ternary to avoid this.

sections.content: When two sibling components need to share data, lift the state up to their common parent. The parent holds the state and passes it down as props with callback functions for children to update it.

exercises.question: When two sibling components need to share state, where should the state live?
options: In their closest common parent component
exercises.correctAnswer: In their closest common parent component
hints: State needs to be accessible to all components that need it
exercises.explanation: Lifting state to the closest common ancestor is the standard React pattern. The parent owns the state and passes it down via props to both siblings.

capstoneProject.title: Task Manager App
capstoneProject.description: Build a full-featured task manager with add, complete, filter, and delete functionality.
requirements: Add task form (controlled input, validates empty string)
Task list renders from state array with keys
Complete toggle (checkbox or click) updates task status
Delete button removes task from state immutably
Filter buttons (All/Active/Completed) — state lifted to parent
Task count display (X of Y tasks remaining)
Empty state message when no tasks match filter
